frontmatter_description: Judge the most likely or most natural answer from how common or typical a category, outcome, or reaction usually is, rather than from a vague quantifier word or a freshly observed sample count.
title: Base Rate and Typicality
use_when: Use when the question asks which outcome, category, trait, role, or reaction is most likely, given how common or typical it usually is.
Use when the answer is the default emotional or behavioral reaction a normal person has to an ordinary event (gift, win, loss, threat), and no twist makes the situation unusual.
Use when a vivid individual description must be weighed against a stated population frequency or prior category prevalence.
Use when the inference is about prior likelihood before any decisive direct observation settles the case.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the task is to recover the approximate range a quantifier word implies (some, most, almost all, about half). That is about word meaning, not category likelihood. Handle that with the vague-quantity interpretation skill.

Do not use when a specific sample, partial count, or newly seen subset was observed and the estimate must be revised on that data. Observed-sample updating is the closest neighbor and the main confusion; route it to the quantity-update-after-observation skill.
Do not use when the question asks what caused an outcome rather than which outcome was more likely beforehand. Naming a cause is causal attribution.
Do not use when the decisive variable is a character's belief, perception, or intention rather than objective base rate; use the matching belief, perception, or intention skill.
Do not use when an explicit fact in the story already settles the answer, so the prior is irrelevant.
decision_variable: how common or typical the category, outcome, or reaction is by default, used as a prior with no specific sample observed
trigger_checklist: The question asks what is most likely, most probable, typical, expected, natural, or common.
The decisive cue is a prior: a stated population frequency, role frequency, ordinary prevalence, or the default reaction to a familiar event.
No specific sample was observed in the scene that would force the estimate to be revised on that data.
The answer is a default given what is usual, not a quantifier word's meaning and not a cause.
Any vivid individual description present is representative or stereotype-like, not specifically diagnostic.
workflow: Confirm the operation is a prior-likelihood judgment: no observed sample to update on, no quantifier word to decode, no cause to name. If any of those, exit (see Boundary Exit Rule).
Name the candidate categories, outcomes, or reactions being compared.
Find the prior: a stated frequency or population proportion if given, otherwise the default or most usual case for this ordinary situation.
For a normal event with no twist, pick the typical reaction a normal person would have (a longed-for gift gives happiness, a win gives pride, a threat gives fear).

If a vivid description is present, test it: is it specifically diagnostic of the rare category, or merely representative? If merely representative, keep the base rate central and do not switch to the rare category.
Choose the higher-prior option. State it as more likely or expected, not certain, unless an explicit fact in the scene makes it decisive.

special_case.title: Vivid or stereotypical description versus base rate
special_case.rule: When a vivid description resembles a rare category but the stated base rate strongly favors a common one, stay with the common category unless the description is specifically diagnostic rather than merely representative. Resemblance alone does not beat a strong prior.

worked_example.scene: At a conference there are 90 engineers and 10 poets. Alex is described as quiet, precise, and fond of notebooks.
worked_example.question: Is Alex more likely to be an engineer or a poet?
worked_example.answer_logic: The quiet-notebook description feels poet-like, but it is representative, not diagnostic; many engineers fit it too. The 90-to-10 base rate dominates, so engineer is more likely. Note this is a pure prior judgment: nothing was sampled and no count needs revising, which is what separates it from updating-on-observed-data.

boundary_exit_rule: If the core operation is mapping a quantifier word (many, few, most, about half) onto an approximate range, that is decoding word meaning, not comparing category likelihood; use the vague-quantity interpretation skill.

If a specific sample, partial count, or newly seen subset was observed and the estimate must be revised on that data, that is updating a count from observation; use the quantity-update-after-observation skill. The tell: the scene reports something just seen (8 of 10 were flu) that should move the number.
If the question asks what produced the result, that is causal attribution.
If the issue is what a character thinks is likely rather than what is objectively likely from base rates, use the matching belief or knowledge skill.
If the prior judgment is only one substep inside a larger negotiation, trust, false-belief, or communication scene, hand back to the macro route that owns that scene.

references.route_signal: Use this unit when likelihood turns on a prior: commonness, category frequency, ordinary prevalence, or the default reaction to a familiar event, with no specific sample observed to update on.
hard_boundary: This unit judges category or reaction likelihood from a prior, not the approximate range of a quantifier word.
This unit uses a standing base rate, not revision on a freshly observed sample; if a count was just seen and must move the estimate, that is the updating neighbor, not this unit.
This unit does not assign causation, blame, responsibility, or moral fault.
This unit does not infer hidden beliefs or intentions unless they only serve as evidence for a likelihood comparison.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not pick the option that sounds most vivid, narratively interesting, or stereotype-matching while ignoring a stated base rate.
Do not treat typicality as certainty; the common case can still be wrong for a particular individual.
Do not silently turn a prior into a posterior: if the scene reports an observed sample, you have left this unit.
common_failure_modes: Base-rate neglect: choosing a rare category because a vivid description resembles it.
Overcorrection: clinging to the base rate even when the scene gives explicitly diagnostic individuating evidence.
Treating an observed sample as if it were a base rate, or vice versa, instead of updating when data was actually seen.
Confusing frequency with cause: assuming the commonest factor must have caused the event.

minimal_pair.case: A clinic usually sees flu and cold cases about equally. With no patients yet examined today, which is more likely to walk in next?
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Pure prior: the standing base rate is the only cue and nothing has been observed, so this is base-rate reasoning, this unit.

minimal_pair.case: Same clinic, but today 8 of the first 10 patients tested flu-positive; should the flu estimate be revised upward?
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: A specific sample was just observed and must move the estimate. Single variable changed (observed data now exists), and that routes to the quantity-update-after-observation skill, not here.

minimal_pair.case: A teacher says most students submitted the form; what approximate share is that?
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The task is decoding the quantifier word most, not comparing category likelihoods, so it routes to the vague-quantity interpretation skill.

boundary_stress_test: Vivid but non-diagnostic description plus a strong stated base rate: keep the base rate central (stay in this unit).
A random draw from a population with known proportions: use those proportions (this unit).
A new sample such as 8 of 10 observed cases is reported: you are now updating on data, so hand off to the observed-sample updating skill.
A character directly saw the answer: perception settles it; do not override it with typicality.
references.generalization_note: Prior-likelihood reasoning is not only numeric puzzles: the typical emotional reaction to an ordinary event, expected social roles, everyday risk, group membership, and likely behavior all rest on base rate or typicality when direct evidence is incomplete.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A case asks for the most likely category, outcome, or default reaction, decided by a stated frequency or by what is typical given an ordinary event, with no observed sample.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A case asks what many, few, most, or about half means as an approximate quantity range.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A case reports a specific observed sample that should revise an estimate, or asks what caused an outcome rather than which outcome was likely beforehand.

notes: Keep the output probabilistic: say more likely, less likely, or expected, not guaranteed.
Use stated base rates before social stereotypes unless the story gives diagnostic individuating evidence.
When a larger estimation scene needs a base-rate substep, this unit can serve as that substep and then return control to the owning scene.
core_question: Judge likelihood from commonness or typicality
